newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-July CPI data curbs Spain's rate cut scope.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-July CPI data curbs Spain's rate cut scope.

text.p: Spain said on Wednesday that inflation remained subdued in July, but evidence of surging prices in some areas fanned concern the central bank may only have limited room to cut key money rates.
Headline inflation rose 0.2 percent month-on-month, or 1.6 percent year-on-year, which as most analysts had expected was unchanged from the previous month's level.
But core inflation, which excludes the volatile energy and fresh food sectors, rose by 2.0 percent year-on-year, which was at the top end of analysts forecasts.
"The rebound in core inflation is worrying...It shows that structural reforms still remain to be done," said an economist at Capital Markets in Madrid.

After some months of positive economic surprises from Spain in terms of price data, the July numbers show real signs of an economic pick-up, furthering the argument that more structural reforms are required if a sharp decline in inflation since last year is to be consolidated.
Moreover, tourism and services prices picked up sharply, with economists citing the impact of a newly fortified sterling and dollar versus the peseta, amongst other factors.

Services inflation excluding rents rose 0.7 percent from June, producing a 3.7 percent year-on-year rate, while tourism and hotel prices gained 1.6 percent from the previous month, up 4.3 percent year-on-year.

"Services inflation is pretty horrendous really...with a good tourist season and strong sterling, people are on a spending spree and (in Spain) they're taking advantage to put their prices up," said Colin Warren at Tokai Bank, London.
On top of this, consumer confidence is on the rise after labour market reform boosted perceptions of job security, making consumers more willing to spend.
Strong economic growth anticipated in the second half of the year may mean that the central bank's scope for cutting key money rates from the present 5.25 percent are scanty.

"Headline (inflation) rates have come down but they've made no progress on the services and tourism front...This makes the Bank of Spain's task more difficult. If we weren't in a situation where they have to converge (for monetary union) people would be talking about them taking the heat out of the recovery," Tokai's Warren added.
Energy prices were another potential danger, and some economists were considering revising upwards their year-end inflation forecast.

"With this rise in services, together with the dollar's rise and the increase in energy costs we are worried that by the end of the year we may revise up our forecast for a two percent year-on-year inflation rate," said Yolanda Fernandez, an economist at AFI Madrid.
Overhanging all of this is the possibility that the Bundesbank may soon raise German money rates, thus limiting the Spanish central bank's scope.
But one bond analyst said that, in a way, this makes the Bank of Spain's limited room to manoeuvre more palatable.

"The Bank of Spain is going to have a hard time cutting rates. But it depends on the Buba. If Germany doesn't move soon, we may see another 25 basis point cut. But if the Buba hikes rates, the Bank of Spain would hold at 5.25 percent for a long time, which would make life easier. (Governor Luis Angel) Rojo will stay prudent, I think," he said.
